newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Papua New Guinea's leader prays for unity.
newsitem.headline: Papua New Guinea's leader prays for unity.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's new leader on Sunday pleaded for unity among his people as the South Pacific nation returns to calm after weathering its worst political crisis in 22 years of independence.

Caretaker Prime Minister John Giheno said in a public message on Easter that his country must learn from the recent crisis, which forced Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan out of office after mutinous troops blockaded parliament.
"My plea to all leaders at all levels of government and public office holders is that we cannot take for granted the events of the past few days and let these slip by to memory lane," he said.
"The experiences should now make us uphold integrity of office.
"We hope and pray that God gives us the wisdom to exercise our powers with dignity."
Giheno on Saturday declared his confidence in the loyalty of the military, but said it would take time to repair the damaged relations between the army and the government.
"We have every confidence in the military for them to do the right thing," Giheno, who was sworn in on Thursday, told Reuters.
"I will try to ease the situation as fast as possible to restore (good relations)."
The crisis erupted earlier this month when military chief Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok condemned Chan's plan to use mercenaries to quell a secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island.
Singirok demanded Chan's ousting and an inquiry into the awarding of the $36 million mercenary contract.
Chan sacked Singirok, but opposition to the deal sparked 10 days of turmoil in which thousands protested in the streets and members of the army mutinied.

An Australian newspaper on Sunday reported mercenary leader retired British Colonel Tim Spicer will accuse senior government officials of skimming millions of dollars from the mercenary deal when he gives evidence before the inquiry, due to begin on Tuesday.
The Melbourne-based Herald Sun, quoting sources, said Spicer was preparing evidence that pointed to millions in cash being skimmed.
Spicer is being held in Papua New Guinea for trial next month on two illegal firearms charges. The remaining 70 mercenaries have left the country.
Chan stepped aside on Wednesday, pending the outcome of the inquiry, in a bid to defuse the volatile situation.
But because he did not resign Chan can resume power if the inquiry clears him before the regular national election in June, although most analysts say there is not enough time.

Giheno has described the soldiers' actions as mutiny and said they should be charged. But he said the cabinet would decide, possibly next week, if the troops should be prosecuted or pardoned in line with a request by Singirok.
The cabinet will also consider what to do with a planeload of weapons and equipment seized by Australia at Port Moresby's request.
Giheno said some of the helicopters and weapons destined for the mercenary operation may be given to the ill-equipped police and the rest could be sold.
"It will be up to cabinet to decide," he said.
